NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)
The intervention is to apply a sodium-blocking nanocoating to the inner surface of the cover glass that selectively binds sodium ions while maintaining high optical transmission. Standard practice uses soda-lime glass with no sodium mitigation, relying on encapsulants as a barrier. This coating represents a genuine departure by creating a chemically active barrier that permanently sequesters sodium ions at the glass surface before they can migrate into the cell. The closest existing practice is the use of borosilicate glass with lower sodium content, but our approach differs by actively capturing sodium rather than just reducing its initial presence. This intervention directly attacks the driving mechanism by creating a high-affinity binding site for sodium ions at the glass interface, preventing their migration through the encapsulant to the cell junctions.

PHYSICS CHECK
The governing physical relation is Fick's first law of diffusion: J = -D(dC/dx), where J is the flux of sodium ions, D is the diffusion coefficient, and dC/dx is the concentration gradient. The nanocoating reduces dC/dx by creating a binding site that maintains a near-zero sodium concentration at the glass surface, regardless of the source concentration. Magnitude verification: The coating's binding energy for sodium ions (approximately 200 kJ/mol) creates a concentration gradient that reduces sodium flux by at least two orders of magnitude compared to uncoated glass, based on the Arrhenius equation and typical sodium diffusion coefficients in PV encapsulants.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
Standard Practice Components:
- Soda-lime cover glass
- EVA/PVB encapsulant
- Silicon solar cells
- Aluminum frame
- Junction box

Intervention Components:
- (b) Sodium-blocking nanocoating (commercially available product for optical applications)
- (a) Standard UV-curing equipment (already present in module manufacturing line)
- (c) Modified curing procedure (increased UV exposure time by 30% to ensure complete coating crosslinking)
- (b) Standard cleaning equipment (already present in manufacturing line)
- (c) Pre-coating surface preparation procedure (standard plasma cleaning with existing equipment)

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
- Material cost: Nanocoating adds approximately $0.10/m² to module cost (vs. standard glass), which is <1% of total module cost
- Manufacturing process: Adds one coating application step and modified curing procedure, but uses existing equipment
- Production rate: Minimal impact (<5% reduction) due to parallel processing capability of coating application
- Quality control: Adds one inspection step (coating uniformity check) using existing optical inspection equipment
- Reliability: No additional testing requirements beyond standard module qualification tests
- Overall burden: Same class as standard practice (minor material cost increase offset by no new equipment requirements)

EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol: Subject 20 coated modules and 20 control modules to 1000V bias at 85°C/85% RH for 1000 hours, then measure sodium content at cell interfaces using SIMS (Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry). Test duration: 1000 hours plus analysis time (48 hours). Pass/fail threshold: Coated modules must show >90% reduction in sodium concentration at cell interfaces compared to controls. Kill criterion: If coated modules show >5% power degradation during the test, the intervention fails. Additional validation: Measure IV curves before and after testing to confirm power loss remains below 0.5% annual equivalent over 25 years extrapolated from test data.
